title: Shankara and the outcaste
word: reading the Isha in the original
hook: an outcaste asks Shankara what exactly should move aside
carry: the same self in every being; don't shrink away
tomorrow: a woman stood up twice to question the wisest man in the room. what did she ask?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the one reality is far, near, and inside all this; that moves and moves not. Today the Isha says what seeing that does to the way you treat people. A great teacher learned it in an alley.
screen: `THAT MOVES. THAT MOVES NOT.` · `NOW: AN ALLEY IN VARANASI.`

segments.voice: Varanasi, early morning, more than a thousand years ago. The young teacher Shankara walks down to bathe in the Ganga, his students around him. In a narrow lane a man blocks the way: a chandala, an outcaste, four dogs at his heels. Shankara says what custom told him to say. Move aside. Move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead. Move what, sir? This body made of food, away from that body made of food? Or the awareness in me, away from the awareness in you? Is the sun any different, shining in the Ganga, or in a puddle in an outcaste's lane?
screen: `VARANASI. THE GANGA. A NARROW LANE.` → `MOVE ASIDE. MOVE WHAT, SIR?` → `THE BODY, OR THE SELF?`

segments.voice: In the traditional telling, Shankara stops. Then he bows, and makes five verses on the spot, each one ending: whoever sees this, outcaste or brahmin, that one is my guru. Some tellings say the man was Shiva himself. Now a verse Shankara himself wrote a commentary on, Isha six. Yas tu sarvani bhutany atmany evanupashyati, sarvabhuteshu catmanam. Whoever keeps seeing all beings in the self, and the self in all beings. Hear the mirror: beings, self; self, beings. Anupashyati isn't a glance. It means keeps seeing. Then: tato na vijugupsate. From that, one shrinks from no one. Verse seven adds: for one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what confusion, what grief? This is one of the biggest teachings in Hinduism: the atman, the self, is the same light in every being. Advaita teachers read it as one self in all. Devotional teachers read it as the Lord living in every heart. Either way, the outcaste's question lands. You can't keep this verse and still flinch from a person. Many Hindu teachers retell the story to say it plainly: no human being is untouchable. And it reaches small places too. The kid everyone scoots away from at lunch. The man on the bus talking to nobody. The verse doesn't ask you to like everyone. It asks you to see who's there.
screen: `HE BOWS: THAT ONE IS MY GURU.` · `SELF IN ALL: SHRINK FROM NONE.` · `ATMAN: THE SAME LIGHT IN ALL.` · `NO ONE IS UNTOUCHABLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you passed today: a neighbor, a driver, someone you ignored, someone who annoyed you. For each one, say inwardly: the same self in them. If you pray, fold your hands for each, the way Hindus do in namaste, a bow to the one in front of you. Keep going as long as the breaths allow.
Reading the Isha in the original, verse six: na vijugupsate. Whoever sees the self in every being shrinks from no one.
